lines.text: Your family needs bread, but grinding grain by hand takes hours every day.
So you crush grain between two flat stones, back and forth, until your arms ache.
But by evening, you've made barely enough flour for one loaf.
Then you notice the stream rushing past your house, shoving hard at every rock.
So you cut planks and build a big wooden wheel with flat paddles around the rim.
You push a thick log through the middle as an axle and rest it on two posts.
The current pushes the bottom paddles, and the wheel starts to turn.
But only the push helps, and most of the stream's power slips away.
So you dig a channel upstream and build a wooden trough that pours water over the top of the wheel.
You swap the paddles for buckets. Falling water fills them, and its weight drags the wheel around. This is an overshot wheel.
Engineers later measured wheels like this at about sixty five percent efficient, over twice the old kind.
But your wheel spins upright, and a millstone has to spin flat.
So you fix a toothed wheel to the axle, and its teeth drive a small flat toothed drum. These are gears.
On the drum's shaft, you set a heavy round millstone above a fixed stone.
You hang a wooden hopper over it, and grain trickles into the hole in the middle.
The stream turns the wheel, the gears turn the stone, and flour spills out the edge. This is a water mill.
By ten eighty six, one English survey counted over six thousand mills.
Congratulations. You have built a water mill.
